newsitem.title: USA: NY mayor moves to reform police relations.
newsitem.headline: NY mayor moves to reform police relations.

text.p: Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, facing an uproar over the alleged sexual torture of a Haitian man at a police station, Tuesday introduced a new task force that included critics of his handling of police brutality charges.

The group was being established to improve communication between police and the communities they patrol, Giuliani said at a news conference he hosted along with urban leaders, advocates and frequent critics such as Norman Siegel, head of the New York Civil Liberties Union.

With Giuliani and Police Commissioner Howard Safir standing next to him at City Hall, Siegel said the scope of the group needed to be broadened to tackle the difficult issues of brutality and racism in the force of 38,000 New York City police officers.
"We must once and for all develop a comprehensive program to realistically ameliorate police brutality" and "confront the systemic problems about police brutality," Siegel said.

In another response to the alleged beating and sexual torture of Haitian immigrant Abner Louima by officers 10 days ago, Safir said he was placing more black and Hispanic cops at the precinct where the alleged assault took place.

Four officers from the 70th precinct in Brooklyn have been arrested and arraigned for the Aug. 9 incident that highlighted three years of increased allegations of police abuses in minority communities.
Two officers have been arraigned on charges of assault for allegedly beating Louima after his arrest following a scuffle outside a nightclub.

Two others have been charged with aggravated sexual abuse and assault for allegedly inserting the wooden handle of a toilet plunger up his rectum and afterwards shoving it in his mouth. Louima said the officers yelled racial slurs at him during the attack.
Louima, a 30-year-old security guard with no criminal record, suffered severe internal injuries and his attorneys said Tuesday they expected him to remain in the hospital for a further three months.
Louima and his wife Michelene have filed a $55 million suit against the city for physical and psychological injuries.
One of his attorneys Tuesday alleged that Louima had been left for dead in the precinct house without treatment.

"If someone is left lying in a cell with severe injuries for an hour and a half in a pool of blood while he is groaning in agony asking for an ambulance and police officers are walking up and down ignoring this ... it speaks volumes about what the intent was," attorney Carl Thomas told a news conference.
The latest move by Giuliani, who has built his mayorship since 1994 on bringing crime down to its lowest levels in a generation, did not satisfy some critics.

"While we welcome every effort by the mayor to address the issue, we feel that nothing short of an independent inquiry is required," said Roger Rathman, spokesman for the human rights group Amnesty International.
The group issued a scathing report 14 months ago on the rising number of complaints against officers. It said blacks, Hispanics and Asians were disproportionaty the victims of abuses.
